evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: The document cites prior literature (refs 16-17) on racial/ethnic differences in LD surveillance case counts and disease severity at diagnosis as rationale for collecting race/ethnicity data, but does not report cost findings stratified by race/ethnicity within this cohort.

The Methods note that costs 'possibly incurred during diagnostic workup before an LD diagnosis' were captured by including the 30 days before the index date in the follow-up window, implying a diagnostic-delay-related cost burden, but this is not separately quantified as a distinct diagnostic-delay cost.

Indirect costs (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) are mentioned only as an explicit exclusion ('This estimation does not include all states or indirect costs') and are not measured anywhere in the study.
The Discussion notes 'the need for effective preventive measures to reduce costs,' implying a prevention/public-health burden dimension, but no prevention cost-effectiveness figures are modeled.
evidence_gaps: No measurement of indirect costs (lost income, productivity loss, unpaid caregiving time) for LD patients or their families - the authors state this explicitly as excluded from their extrapolation.

The 6-month follow-up period is stated by the authors as potentially 'too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms,' so costs for prolonged or relapsing post-treatment symptoms beyond 6 months are not captured.

Cost extrapolation is limited to the 16 high-incidence states/DC; the authors state LD case-identification algorithm was validated only in high-incidence states, so no extrapolated national (all-50-state) total cost figure is provided.

The claims-based localized/disseminated classification algorithm itself 'has not been validated,' per the authors, so misclassification between these cost-driving subgroups may affect the magnitude of cost differences reported.

The study population is limited to insured patients within Optum Market Clarity and 'may not be generalizable to all patients with LD,' per the authors' own stated limitation, leaving costs for uninsured or non-claims-captured patients unmeasured.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the four cost-estimation methods (LD episode analysis, cases-as-self-controls, case-control, multivariable-adjusted) into one single point estimate or simple low-to-high confidence range: they differ in population size (70,531 all cases for episode analysis; 64,893 continuously-enrolled cases for self-controls; 64,891 cases vs 168,509 controls for case-control/multivariable) and in measurement time window (episode analysis uses variable-length LD episodes, potentially extending beyond 1 year and excluding pharmacy costs; self-controls and case-control/multivariable analyses use a fixed 6-month baseline vs 6-month follow-up window and include pharmacy costs). These are structurally different measurements of related but non-identical cost concepts, not merely different confidence levels on one estimate.

Do not add patient OOP costs to the estimated 'direct' (standardized/allowed-amount) costs reported in this study; the authors explicitly state 'This study did not compare OOP costs to the estimated direct costs because OOP costs were not standardized,' and OOP amounts are a subset/component of what plans and patients jointly pay, not an addition on top of direct costs.

Extrapolated national-scale costs ($591 million-$1.05 billion) apply only to the 16 LD high-incidence states/DC and only to health care costs - not indirect costs, not non-high-incidence states, and not a lifetime cost (it is an annual estimate only).

Comparator studies discussed (Zhang et al. 2000 data, Hook et al. 2014-2016 data, Adrion et al. 2006-2010 data), even after the authors' own CPI-adjustment to 2022 dollars, used different populations (e.g., Adrion restricted to commercially insured patients younger than 65; Hook used patient-reported/verified utilization data in 4 high-incidence states only), different time periods, and different cost-estimation methods, so they should not be pooled with this study's current-cohort estimates as if directly comparable.

LD-specific costs (ICD-10 A69.xx claims only, excluding pharmacy) and all-cause total health care costs (including pharmacy and non-LD-related care) are two distinct cost perspectives used in different analyses within this study and should not be combined or treated as interchangeable.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The cohort was 51.3% female and 48.7% male overall (Table 1); sex composition was also reported by LD classification subgroup (e.g., 57.7% female among indeterminate-disease cases vs ~50% female among localized and disseminated cases). This is a demographic/compositional breakdown; the document does not report cost or burden outcomes stratified by sex.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Case identification, classification (localized/disseminated/indeterminate), and all cost outcomes in this study are derived from ICD-10 LD diagnosis codes (A69.xx) and antibiotic prescriptions within Optum Market Clarity, an integrated medical claims, pharmacy claims, and EHR dataset - a claims/ICD-10-coded source, not prospective surveillance or a symptom-based case definition. The authors themselves note the underlying CDC claims-based algorithm has limitations and 'may not be generalizable to all patients with LD.'

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The headline direct and OOP cost estimates across all four methods (LD episode cost of $2,227; self-controls difference of $3,304; case-control difference of $4,098; multivariable-adjusted difference of $5,571) are reported pooled nationally and by LD classification subgroup (localized/disseminated/indeterminate) and by state LD-incidence status, but are not reported disaggregated by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status. Age, sex, race, and ethnicity were used only as adjustment covariates in the multivariable model, not as reported stratified cost outputs.

decision_relevance.summary: A simulator built from this document could let payers/policy analysts explore how projected national or state-level Lyme disease cost burden changes under different assumed case counts or disease-severity mixes (localized vs disseminated vs indeterminate), using the study's own per-episode and per-patient cost inputs. spec.title: Lyme Disease Direct Health Care Cost Explorer (Claims-Based, 2016-2022)
spec.boundary: This simulator models only direct health care cost figures reported in a claims/EHR-based cohort study (Optum Market Clarity, 2016-2022, 2022 dollars). It does not add indirect costs (lost income, caregiving time), does not extend beyond the study's own 6-month or variable-length episode windows, and does not combine out-of-pocket costs with direct costs, per the study's own stated limitation that out-of-pocket amounts were not standardized. The episode-based cost method and the multivariable-adjusted 6-month method are kept as separate, non-interchangeable groups rather than pooled into one figure.

takeaway.patient: In this large U.S. insurance claims dataset (2016-2022, costs in 2022 dollars), the typical standardized direct medical cost per Lyme disease episode was about $695 for localized disease versus about $6,833 for disseminated (more widely spread) disease - a difference of about $6,138, with disseminated disease costing roughly 9.8 times as much. Among the smaller subset of patients with recorded out-of-pocket data (about 15.5% of all cases), out-of-pocket spending averaged about $188 per episode. These are claims-based figures for insured patients only; the study reports an association between disease stage at diagnosis and cost, but did not test whether earlier diagnosis itself lowers a given patient's costs, and it does not include lost income, caregiving time, or costs beyond about six months to a year.
takeaway.care: Among 70,531 Lyme disease patients identified via ICD-10 claims codes (2016-2022, 2022 dollars), standardized direct medical costs per episode were markedly higher for disseminated disease (~$6,833) than localized disease (~$695), a difference of about $6,138 using the episode-based costing method. Using a separate multivariable-adjusted method comparing all-cause 6-month costs to matched controls, the projected cost increase for disseminated-disease patients was about $10,263 larger than the adjusted increase for Lyme patients overall ($15,834 vs $5,571 per patient over 6 months). The study reports this as an association observed in claims data between disease classification at diagnosis and subsequent cost, not a test of whether changing diagnostic timing changes outcomes or costs for a given patient; the claims-based localized/disseminated classification algorithm itself has not been independently validated.
takeaway.policy: This claims-based study (Optum Market Clarity, 2016-2022, 70,531 identified Lyme disease cases, costs in 2022 dollars) estimated about 295,339 annual Lyme disease cases in 16 high-incidence states and DC, derived from a national case estimate (476,000, cited from Kugeler et al. 2021), an 81% high-incidence-state share, and a 0.766 case-definition positive predictive value (cited from Kluberg et al. 2025) - none measured directly by this study. Applying two of the study's four cost-estimation methods to that case count, the study reports total annual Lyme disease-associated direct health care costs of $591 million to $1.05 billion in those states. A multivariable-adjusted model separately projected Lyme disease cases had about $5,571 higher all-cause 6-month costs per patient than matched controls overall, rising to about $15,834 for disseminated disease - a difference of about $10,263. These figures cover direct health care costs only, exclude indirect costs, and apply only to insured, claims-captured populations in high-incidence states.

patient: When discussing possible Lyme disease symptoms with a clinician, ask whether the illness appears localized or has spread, since this study found much higher claims-based costs when disease was more advanced at the time of diagnosis.

If out-of-pocket cost is a concern, ask your own insurer what Lyme-related care it covers, since this study found an average out-of-pocket cost of about $188 per episode among a subset of insured patients - your own plan and situation may differ.
Keep in mind this study does not include lost income, caregiving time, or costs beyond about six months to a year, so it will not capture your full financial picture if symptoms are prolonged.
care: The cost gap this study associates with localized versus disseminated disease classification may be worth reviewing against your own practice's diagnostic and referral timelines, keeping in mind the claims-based classification algorithm itself has not been independently validated per the study's authors.

Consider whether your care pathway has a clear point of coordination for patients who may be progressing from a localized to a disseminated presentation, given the size of the cost difference associated with disease stage at diagnosis.

When communicating these figures internally, keep the episode-based and multivariable-adjusted estimates separate, since they use different populations, time windows, and cost scopes and should not be combined into one number.
policy: Use the case-count and cost-per-case figures here for scenario planning around Lyme disease program budgets in high-incidence states, treating the $591M-$1.05B range as spanning two different estimation methods rather than a single point estimate.

When citing the extrapolated case count, note it depends on externally cited estimates (national case incidence, high-incidence-state share, case-definition positive predictive value) rather than a value this study measured directly.

package.documentation:
This simulator is based on Yu et al. (JAMA Network Open, 2026), a retrospective cohort study using Optum Market Clarity U.S. medical/pharmacy claims and EHR data (2016-2022) on 70,531 patients with a Lyme disease (LD) diagnosis, compared with matched controls and with themselves (pre/post). All dollar figures are CPI-adjusted to 2022 dollars.

The study uses four distinct cost-estimation methods - LD-specific episode costs, self-controlled baseline-vs-follow-up comparison, unadjusted case-control comparison, and multivariable-adjusted case-control comparison - which differ in population, time window (variable-length LD episodes vs fixed 6-month windows), and pharmacy-cost inclusion. This simulator keeps the episode-based inputs (localized/disseminated per-episode cost) and the multivariable-adjusted inputs (overall/disseminated cost difference) as separate, non-interchangeable groups rather than pooling them, and never adds out-of-pocket cost to direct cost, per the study's own stated limitation that out-of-pocket amounts were not standardized.

The extrapolated case count (about 295,339 annual cases in 16 high-incidence states and DC) reproduces the study's own stated multiplication of a national annual case estimate (476,000, cited by the study from Kugeler et al. 2021), a high-incidence-state share (81%), and a case-definition positive predictive value (0.766, cited from Kluberg et al. 2025); none of these three component figures were directly measured by this study.

Limitations: Case identification, disease classification, and all cost outcomes rely on ICD-10 diagnosis codes (A69.xx) and claims/EHR data rather than prospective surveillance, so the figures likely undercount true Lyme disease burden and may not generalize beyond insured, claims-captured patients. The headline cost figures are reported pooled nationally and by disease classification and state incidence status, but have not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity within this study - federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports that kind of disaggregated analysis even though this study did not perform it. The cohort was 51.3% female and 48.7% male overall, with a higher female share (57.7%) specifically among indeterminate-classification cases; the study does not report cost outcomes stratified by sex. The study explicitly excludes indirect costs (lost income, caregiving time) and costs beyond its 6-month-to-episode-length windows, and its own localized/disseminated classification algorithm has not been independently validated.

Consider whether your care pathway has a clear point of coordination for patients who may be progressing from a localized to a disseminated presentation, given the size of the cost difference associated with disease stage at diagnosis.

When communicating these figures internally, keep the episode-based and multivariable-adjusted estimates separate, since they use different populations, time windows, and cost scopes and should not be combined into one number.
policy: Use the case-count and cost-per-case figures here for scenario planning around Lyme disease program budgets in high-incidence states, treating the $591M-$1.05B range as spanning two different estimation methods rather than a single point estimate.

When citing the extrapolated case count, note it depends on externally cited estimates (national case incidence, high-incidence-state share, case-definition positive predictive value) rather than a value this study measured directly.

Consider that this claims-based cohort likely undercounts true Lyme disease burden and has not been checked for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; federal survey data such as NHIS or BRFSS could support that kind of disaggregated analysis alongside this claims-based estimate.

inputs.label: Localized disease direct cost per episode
inputs.source: Document Results 'LD Episode Analysis' and Table 2; 400-900 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported mean direct, claims-standardized medical cost per Lyme disease episode among patients classified as localized disease; moving it changes the severity cost gap and ratio outputs below.

inputs.label: Disseminated disease direct cost per episode
inputs.source: Document Results 'LD Episode Analysis' and Table 2; 5000-9000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported mean direct cost per episode for patients classified with disseminated (more widely spread) Lyme disease; its range is kept above the localized-cost range so the sliders cannot contradict the study's own finding that disseminated disease cost more in every reported comparison.

inputs.label: Adjusted all-cause 6-month cost difference, overall
inputs.source: Document Results 'Multivariable Analysis' and Table 5; 3000-6000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's model-projected mean difference in all-cause 6-month health care costs between Lyme disease cases overall and matched controls, adjusted for demographics, comorbidity, and baseline cost; it uses a different measurement window than the episode-based costs above.

inputs.label: Adjusted all-cause 6-month cost difference, disseminated disease
inputs.source: Document Results 'Multivariable Analysis' and Table 5; 10000-20000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the same adjusted model's projected cost difference restricted to disseminated-disease cases; its range is kept above the overall-adjusted-difference range so the sliders cannot contradict the study's finding that disseminated disease carried a larger adjusted cost increase.

inputs.label: Estimated annual U.S. Lyme disease cases (cited)
inputs.source: Document Results 'Extrapolation to High-Incidence States', p.10 and eTable 12, citing Kugeler et al. 2021; 300000-600000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is a national Lyme disease case estimate the study cites from another study (Kugeler et al. 2021) as the starting point for its own extrapolation; moving it changes the estimated high-incidence-state case count below.

inputs.label: Share of U.S. cases in high-incidence states
inputs.source: Document Results 'Extrapolation to High-Incidence States', p.10 and eTable 12; 0.7-0.9 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the cited share of estimated U.S. Lyme disease cases attributed to the 16 high-incidence states and DC; it scales the estimated case count output below.

inputs.label: Case-definition positive predictive value (cited)
inputs.source: Document Results 'Extrapolation to High-Incidence States', p.10 and eTable 12, citing Kluberg et al. 2025; 0.6-0.9 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is a cited estimate of how often the claims-based case definition correctly identifies a true Lyme disease case; it reduces the raw national case estimate to account for possible misclassification in the extrapolation below.

inputs.label: Patient out-of-pocket cost per episode, overall
inputs.source: Document Results 'LD Episode Analysis' and Table 2; 100-400 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported mean patient out-of-pocket cost per Lyme disease episode, measured only among the roughly 15.5% of case patients with recorded out-of-pocket claims data; the study states it was not combined with the direct-cost figures elsewhere because out-of-pocket amounts were not standardized.

outputs.label: Disseminated minus localized direct cost per episode (positive = disseminated costs more)
outputs.interpretation: This is the dollar difference between the study's reported mean direct cost per episode for disseminated versus localized Lyme disease, both from the same episode-based costing method. A larger value reflects a bigger claims-based cost difference associated with disease classification at diagnosis; the study reports this as an observed association, not a test of whether earlier treatment prevents the difference.

outputs.label: Disseminated divided by localized direct cost per episode
outputs.interpretation: This expresses the disseminated-disease episode cost as a multiple of the localized-disease episode cost from the same method. At the study's own default values this computes to about 9.8, meaning disseminated-disease episodes cost roughly ten times as much as localized-disease episodes in this claims cohort.

outputs.label: Adjusted disseminated minus adjusted overall 6-month cost difference (positive = disseminated patients' adjusted cost increase exceeds the overall average)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the study's projected adjusted all-cause cost increase for disseminated-disease cases and the adjusted increase for Lyme disease cases overall, both from the same multivariable-adjusted model. A larger value indicates the adjusted model attributes a disproportionately larger cost increase specifically to disseminated disease.

outputs.label: Estimated annual Lyme disease cases, high-incidence states
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the study's own stated calculation of estimated annual Lyme disease cases in high-incidence states, multiplying a cited national case estimate by a cited high-incidence-state share and a cited case-definition positive predictive value. At default values it computes to about 295,339, matching the study's own reported figure; it is built from estimates the study cites from other sources, not from this study's own direct measurement.

outputs.label: Patient out-of-pocket cost per episode
outputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported mean out-of-pocket amount patients paid per Lyme disease episode, measured only among the subset (about 15.5%) of case patients with recorded out-of-pocket claims data. The study states this figure was not compared or combined with the direct-cost figures elsewhere because out-of-pocket amounts were not standardized.
